name: Cold sauna (cryotherapy room)

lead: A cold sauna, or whole-body cryotherapy chamber, exposes a lightly clad person to extremely cold air for a few minutes. The cold comes from evaporated liquid nitrogen or from refrigerated air.

Its link to looks is indirect: users, particularly in training communities, use it hoping to reduce muscle soreness and speed recovery so they can train more. Research is strongest for post-exercise soreness and is mixed across other claimed uses.

paras: Users wear minimal clothing with gloves, a headband, mask, and dry shoes and socks. Sessions last roughly two to four minutes, and reviews describe repeated series of sessions over weeks rather than a single visit.

Liquid-nitrogen systems carry risks of frostbite and inert gas asphyxiation. Contraindications listed include cardiovascular disease, high blood pressure, acute infection, seizures and cold allergy. Adverse events are thought to be under-reported.

chain: More muscle and leaner physique over time
angle.text: Users apply it as a recovery tool between training sessions. Any effect on looks runs through training consistency rather than a direct change to the face or body.

lead: Whole-body cryotherapy uses a walk-in chamber that exposes the body to very cold air, below -100 degrees Celsius in many descriptions, for two to four minutes. The cold is produced either by evaporating liquid nitrogen or by refrigerated air.[1]

In looksmaxxing and lifting communities it falls under lifestyle practices. The appearance link is a chain: recovery and reduced soreness, more consistent training, and more muscle and a leaner physique. Wikipedia reports that most evidence for the technique is positive for post-exercise muscle soreness.[1]

The first whole-body chamber was built in Japan in the late 1970s, following the research of rheumatologist Toshima Yamaguchi, reaching Europe in the 1980s and the US and Australia the following decade.[1] The US FDA has said evidence is lacking and more research is needed.[1]
infobox: Liquid nitrogen vapor or refrigerated air

paras: Users enter the chamber wearing minimal clothing plus gloves, a woolen headband, a mask and dry shoes and socks.[1] Shorter exposures are considered more beneficial: three to four minutes versus one to two can reduce thermal sensation, tissue oxygenation and blood volume.[1]
Wikipedia notes that a single session shows little effect and that series of 20 to 30 sessions are recommended in the literature.[1]

Claimed uses include relief from muscle soreness after exercise, rheumatoid arthritis, stress, anxiety, chronic pain, multiple sclerosis and fibromyalgia, with ongoing studies on Alzheimer's disease and migraine.[1] Lifters in strength-training forums discuss cold environments and cold exposure in connection with training and recovery.[2]

A randomized controlled trial in fibromyalgia patients tested whole-body cryotherapy for health-related quality of life, on the expectation that it could ease musculoskeletal pain and fatigue.[3] Reviews describe inconsistent results because chamber types and treatment periods vary, and whole-body cryotherapy is not usually used before performance because it can briefly reduce reflexes, force output and balance.[1]

Liquid-nitrogen systems carry risks of inert gas asphyxiation and frostbite, which electrically operated chambers do not. Contraindications include cardiovascular disease, hypertension, acute infection, seizures, cold allergy and some psychiatric disorders. Reviewers believe adverse events are under-reported.[1]

timeline.event: Yamaguchi's rheumatology research; first whole-body chamber built in Japan.[1]
